title: What does consumer lag tell you, and what does it NOT tell you (per-partition vs aggregate)?
shortTitle: What consumer lag tells you and what it does not (per-partition vs aggregate)
keyPoints: Consumer lag is the difference between the log end offset and the committed offset per partition -- the number of unprocessed records.
Near-zero lag means the consumer is keeping up; steadily rising lag means it cannot process as fast as records arrive.
Lag is measured in records, not time -- 60 records could be milliseconds or minutes depending on processing cost.
Lag is a level, not a rate -- you need the derivative (rate of change) to know if you are catching up or falling behind.
Aggregate lag hides per-partition problems: 600 total could be 50 on each partition (healthy) or 600 on one stuck partition (incident).
Lag never tells you the cause -- it could be too few consumers, a slow dependency, a hot partition, or a poison pill.
Always monitor lag per partition and by rate of change, not just a single aggregate gauge.

s1_definition.oneliner: Lag tells you the per-partition backlog in records, but not the time delay, the throughput, or the root cause, and an aggregate lag can hide a single stuck partition.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Consumer lag** -- the difference between the log end offset (latest produced record) and the consumer group's committed offset (last acknowledged position) for a partition.
- **Per-partition lag** -- the lag computed individually for each partition, which reveals imbalances and stuck partitions.
- **Aggregate lag** -- the sum of lag across all partitions, which hides per-partition problems because 600 total could be 50 on each or 600 on one.
- **Lag in records vs time** -- lag counts records, not seconds; the actual delay depends on how expensive each record is to process.
- **Rate of change** -- the derivative of lag over time; a constant lag might be fine, but rising lag means the consumer is falling behind.
- **Symptom, not diagnosis** -- lag tells you something is wrong but never why; the cause could be too few consumers, a slow dependency, a hot key, or a poison pill.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine each teller window at National Bank of India has a queue of customers. Consumer lag is the number of customers still waiting at each window. It tells you a window is busy or falling behind. But it does not tell you how long each customer will wait, because one might be a quick balance check and another a complex loan. It does not tell you whether one window is completely jammed while you only look at the total across all windows. And it does not tell you why a window is slow.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Consumer lag is the gap between the latest produced offset and the committed offset per partition, and it is the single most important consumer health signal. Near-zero lag means the consumer is keeping up, steadily rising lag means it cannot process as fast as records arrive, and comparing lag across partitions reveals imbalance.

But lag has critical limitations. It is measured in records, not time, so 60 records could be milliseconds or minutes. It is a level, not a rate, so you need the derivative to know if you are catching up or falling behind. Most dangerously, aggregate lag hides per-partition problems: a total of 600 could be 50 on each partition or 600 on one stuck partition, and the aggregate is identical.

At National Bank of India, the settlement team once watched a single aggregate gauge that read 600 and assumed all was well, while one partition was stuck at 600 and the other eleven were at zero. Pankaj switched to per-partition lag alerting and added time-based lag because some partitions processed cheap records and others hit a slow credit bureau.

Remember one sentence: lag is essential but blunt -- watch it per partition and by rate of change, pair it with time-based lag, and treat it as the alarm that starts an investigation, never as the explanation.
